title: Where Have All the Wasps Gone? Scientists Are Worried
summary:
Have you noticed fewer wasps buzzing around your picnic this summer? You're not alone. In the UK, scientists are worried because wasps seem to be disappearing. Normally, warm weather means more wasps. Last year, newspapers were full of stories about "plagues of wasps." But this summer, even pest controllers say it's quiet. That's a big change.

Wasps might seem annoying, but they are actually important. They help control pests, pollinate flowers, and break down dead plants and animals. Without them, ecosystems could suffer. So why are they missing? The answer may be the weather. Spring 2026 started warm and dry, which is usually good for wasps. New queens, called foundresses, emerge from hibernation and start building nests. But then came extreme heat, followed by cold, damp days and chilly nights. These sudden changes may have killed many queens or caused them to abandon their nests.

Then came the heatwaves. Insects have a temperature limit called critical thermal maximum, or CTmax. If it gets too hot, they can die. For wasps, CTmax is around 45°C (113°F). This summer, ground temperatures in the UK exceeded 50°C. That's hotter than wasps can handle. The few wasps that are still around also seem smaller than usual. Scientists think this is because larvae don't get enough food or develop too fast in the heat, so they end up small.

The Big Wasp Survey will collect data later this summer. If it confirms the drop, it could be a sign of a bigger problem. Wasps are resilient, but even they have limits. So next time a wasp visits your picnic, don't swat it. Watch it. It might be hungry and just trying to survive.
why_it_matters: Small creatures like wasps help keep gardens, farms and parks healthy, so noticing the insects near your own home can tell you a lot about a changing planet.

background_read: The UK, short for the United Kingdom, is a country in Europe made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Wasps belong to the same insect family as bees and ants. There are many different kinds of wasps, and most of them never bother people at all.

Insects all over the world are having a hard time because of hotter weather, less rain and the loss of the plants they live on. Scientists count the same insects year after year to see whether their numbers are going up or down.
Article_Structure: WHO: Wasps in the UK — and the scientists and pest controllers who watch them
WHAT: Wasps seem to be disappearing this summer, even though warm weather usually means more of them
WHERE: In the UK, where ground temperatures went above 50°C
WHY: Wasps pollinate flowers, control pests and break down dead plants and animals, so losing them could hurt whole ecosystems

perspectives.description: Scientists say fewer wasps could mean less help for the plants and crops that depend on insects.
Some people enjoying picnics and barbecues are glad there are fewer wasps around, even if the reason is bad news.
Researchers say the Big Wasp Survey still has to collect its data, so it is too early to be sure the wasps are really vanishing.
